newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa in farm trade drama with United States.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa in farm trade drama with United States.

text.p: Agriculture minister Derek Hanekom pressed his U.S. counterpart Dan Glickman over trade barriers on Monday and said South Africa would launch a major drive to sell farm products to North America.

Hanekom and Glickman, who met during discussions of the U.S.-South Africa binational commission headed by Vice-President Al Gore and Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, told reporters increased trade was in the interests of both countries.
"We want to aggressively target the North American market for our own goods," Hanekom said.
"Historically we've had strong trade links with the European Union, but we think there's a massive potentially opening-up market in the U.S. and Mexico and Canada which hasn't yet been exploited...
"Our main challenge is to show the USA how a real market- based economy works," Hanekom said, referring to U.S. subsidies.
Glickman said the United States was in the process of reducing or removing subsidies on row crops like wheat, corn, cotton and rice.

"We recognise that that will perhaps involve some risk on the part of producers, but in order to counteract that we may have to ensure that markets are free and open for those goods overseas," he said.

"I know that South Africa is participating very strongly with other nations in trying to remove trade barriers and the minister has twisted my arm just a little bit along those lines since I've been here," Glickman said.

South African and U.S. officials said the agriculture committee of the binational commission had removed obstacles to exports of South African citrus and protea flowers to the United States which were based on fears of contamination.
"Since opening the market in July 1996, over 10,000 stems of protea and related flowers and 36,000 tonnes of citrus have entered the U.S. market," a U.S. official said.
The officials said South Africa had agreed to tests for Karnal bunt fungus which would allow in U.S. durum wheat imports, worth an estimated $34 million a year.
Glickman said the United States exported agriculture, fish and forestry products worth $330 million to South Africa last year while importing similar goods worth $121 million from South Arica.
He said trade in farm goods between the two countries had grown 30 percent since 1994, when apartheid was scrapped and trade sanctions were removed.
"There is a great potential for agricultural trade, given the size of our countries. The whole idea is to increase that. This commission is being used to break down bureaucracy," Glickman said.
"I look forward to the day when there will be no barriers between our markets in agricultural products."
